summary: Earth Jukebox is a browser app that lets people hear NASA’s pictures of Earth. It takes visualizations from NASA’s Earth Information Center and Worldview and plays them as live music. A playhead sweeps across each image from west to east, reading it as eight horizontal bands: higher in the picture is a higher note, brighter is louder, and warmer colour sounds brighter, with notes kept inside a chosen musical scale. A 3D globe turns under the playhead while eight spikes show each band’s loudness, and a flat map offers the same information. Thirteen tracks cover phenomena such as ocean currents, aerosols, carbon dioxide, night lights and forest height, and NASA’s Caldwell 73 serves as a listening reference. Extras: touch-to-hear probe, guided tour, WAV export. It runs locally in the browser with no logins or API keys, supports keyboard use, screen-reader announcements and reduced motion, and credits every NASA source on screen. The sound comes from the colour and brightness of rendered images
details:
WHAT IT DOES:

Earth Jukebox lets people hear NASA's pictures of Earth. It plays visualizations from NASA's Earth Information Center and Worldview as live music in the browser. A playhead sweeps across the image and reads it as eight horizontal bands: higher in the picture is a higher note, brighter is louder, warmer color sounds brighter. Notes stay inside a musical scale. A 3D globe turns under the playhead, and a flat map shows the same information.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT:

NASA's Earth visuals leave out blind and low-vision people. Earth Jukebox gives them, and anyone who learns by listening, another way to explore oceans, air, forests and city lights, and works as a classroom and outreach tool.

TOOLS:

React, Vite, JavaScript, Three.js and the Web Audio API. Free tools only, running in the browser with no logins or API keys. NASA media is downloaded ahead of time. Parts of the code were written with AI assistance (Claude, Google Antigravity) and reviewed by the team.

CREATIVITY:

The picture is the score: you watch a planet turn under a playhead and hear what you see. The team chose the mapping, scales and looks.

FACTORS CONSIDERED:

The sound comes from colour and brightness in NASA's rendered images, not raw measurements, and the app says so. Globe view is only used for full-world flat maps. Keyboard, screen-reader and reduced-motion support. Every NASA source is credited on screen.
